Triggers.value: Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath
Undergoing a medical examination or procedure

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I think about how life would have been different if the event had not occurred
I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened

Threat.value: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I only feel safe in a very limited number of places

Negative Appraisals.value: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper
I can't trust that I will do the right thing

issues.explanation: 'Arguments' is a weak fit as a primary trigger for PTSD related to a life-threatening illness when the rest of the profile is dominated by somatic danger cues, hypervigilant threat monitoring, and self-appraisals about coping. It is not impossible, but in this profile it appears disconnected from the illness-centered threat pattern and lacks support from memory/appraisal content.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control
issues.explanation: 'Restrict eating to feel in control' is not well integrated with the rest of the formulation. The active edges emphasize threat and negative appraisals leading to maladaptive strategies, but the other selected strategies are cognitive/self-punitive and illness-related themes are otherwise absent from eating control. In this profile it looks like a strategy addressing a different problem domain unless additional body/illness-control content were present.

vignette: The collapse happened during a midnight recording session. One moment Aroha was tracking vocal lines for her chamber ensemble, and the next, a crushing tightness seized her chest. The studio's HVAC system exhaled a sterile chemical draft that made her throat spasm. Paramedics arrived with an oxygen mask and an intubation tube; the trauma was not just the suffocation, but the clinical, unyielding pressure of the medical procedure as her airway was forcibly secured. She survived the ICU, but the narrow margin between breath and blackout rewired her nervous system. In the months that followed, her body learned to sound the alarm without her permission. A sudden draft from a car window, a fleeting ache in her ribs, the faint whiff of antiseptic on a stagehand's gloves sparked a visceral flare before her mind could register the context. Her heart hammered while she folded laundry. She woke repeatedly in the dead of night, forcing herself to check the hallway and bedroom door as if confirming the world had not tilted. Over time, the only space where her breathing settled was a corner of her home studio, where she had taped a single acoustic panel around her chair. Outside that perimeter, the air felt treacherous. Because her internal alarm remained locked in overdrive, ordinary sensations suddenly felt like precursors to catastrophe. Walking up stairs to load her cello triggered sharp breathlessness, the very same suffocation that had nearly ended her life. More often, the smell of hospital cleaners or the sterile tang of a bandage roll cut through a rehearsal room, sending her vision tunneling. When a sound engineer applied hand sanitizer near her microphone stand, Aroha would drop her bow and stumble backward, certain the medical procedures that had nearly claimed her were happening again. Her hypervigilance transformed mundane clinical cues into immediate threats. The relentless physiological storms and sleepless nights quickly eroded her self-reliance. She had come to believe she was fundamentally inadequate, that her nervous system had betrayed her when she needed it most. Every time her body reacted to danger before she could process it, she felt like a bad coper, watching her own instrument fail mid-performance. The constant state of alert bred deep self-doubt; she stopped trusting her own judgments about whether she was truly safe or just imagining the worst. The physical reality of her threat response became proof of personal failure. That conviction of inadequacy hardened into rigid behavioral patterns. Because she believed she was a bad coper and could not trust herself with health crises, Aroha began actively avoiding medical cues. She declined routine checkups, cancelled specialist referrals, and drove past urgent care centers en route to studio sessions. She also told herself she deserved the discomfort, framing her anxiety as punishment for failing to prevent the illness. Her counterfactual thinking took root in quiet hours; she replayed the studio's ventilation system, certain life would have been different if she had simply worn a mask. The belief that she was failing at recovery dictated how she lived. The physical urgency of her threat response left her no energy to counter these strategies, only to retreat. When her body reacted with sudden breathlessness or a spike of cortisol during rehearsals, she shut down her instruments and isolated in her safe zone. This avoidance, compounded by her conviction of inadequacy, fractured her professional life. She missed three tour dates, telling her spouse the studio work was overwhelming when the truth was the fear of hospital corridors made her hands shake too violently to hold a bow. The isolation deepened her self-doubt, making every minor chest ache feel like the original collapse returning, which in turn reinforced her certainty that she was utterly inadequate. Now, at forty-six, Aroha sits in her therapist's office, hands resting on her knees, scanning the room for clinical sanitizer. The fear that brought her here is no longer just about collapsing again, but about the slow erosion of the life she loves. She is terrified her body will never trust her, and that she will spend her years confined to a single chair, forever questioning whether she deserved the illness. She hopes, with fragile certainty, that she might finally learn to breathe without bracing for the next attack.
